paragraphs.heading: Telescopes built on mirrors
paragraphs.text: A reflecting telescope, or reflector, uses one or more curved mirrors to reflect light and form an image. Because it relies on mirrors, it is sometimes called a catoptric telescope. Isaac Newton invented it in the 17th century as an alternative to the refracting telescope, which at the time suffered from severe chromatic aberration.

paragraphs.heading: Why astronomers prefer them
paragraphs.text: Reflectors have optical flaws of their own, but the design allows objectives of very large diameter. Almost all the major telescopes used in astronomy research are reflectors, from the Hubble Space Telescope down to small amateur models. The same principle works at other wavelengths too; X-ray telescopes also use reflection to form images. Reflectors handle a wider range of light, since glass elements in a lens absorb certain wavelengths. And while a lens must be flawless through its whole volume, a mirror needs only one perfectly polished surface.

paragraphs.heading: From idea to first instrument
paragraphs.text: The idea that curved mirrors act like lenses is at least as old as Alhazen, whose optics treatise dates from the 11th century. Soon after the refracting telescope appeared, Galileo, Giovanni Francesco Sagredo and others discussed building a telescope with a mirror as the objective. Parabolic mirrors promised less spherical aberration and no chromatic aberration, and James Gregory published a design in 1663 that Robert Hooke built in 1673. Still, Newton's telescope of 1668 is considered the first reflector, because earlier designs were never built or failed. It used a spherical metal primary mirror and a small diagonal mirror, a layout now called the Newtonian telescope.

paragraphs.heading: Metal, silver and aluminum
paragraphs.text: From Newton's day to the 19th century, mirrors were made of metal, usually speculum metal. The Leviathan of Parsonstown, the biggest telescope of that century, had a metal mirror 1.8 metres wide. But a speculum mirror lost its shine quickly and reflected just about 2⁄3 of the light, so it had to be re-polished often. Together with the difficulty of building them, this meant reflectors took more than 100 years to catch on. By the mid-19th century cheaper, tarnish-resistant silvered-glass mirrors had become popular, and the 20th century brought long-lasting aluminum coatings.

paragraphs.heading: Modern mirrors
paragraphs.text: Later advances include segmented mirrors that allow larger diameters, and active optics that make up for bending under gravity. Most modern primary mirrors are solid glass cylinders whose front is ground to a spherical or parabolic shape, then coated with a thin vacuum-deposited layer of aluminum. Some are made instead by spinning molten glass so its surface takes a paraboloid shape as it cools, leaving little grinding to do. In the mid-20th century came catadioptric telescopes such as the Schmidt camera, which pair a spherical mirror with a corrector plate lens for wide-field images.

paragraphs.heading: How the light travels
paragraphs.text: The basic element is a curved primary mirror that forms an image at the focal plane; the distance between them is the focal length. Film or a digital sensor can sit there, or a secondary mirror can redirect the light to a sensor or an eyepiece. Because the mirror focuses light at a point in front of itself, almost every design has something near that point partly blocking incoming light. This reduces the light collected and lowers contrast through diffraction, and most supports holding a secondary mirror add diffraction spikes.

paragraphs.heading: Living with imperfection
paragraphs.text: Like any optical system, a reflector never gives a perfect image. Each design must handle objects out to infinity, many wavelengths, and a way to view the primary mirror's image, so it always compromises. Coma keeps central stars sharp but blurs others into comet-like smudges, worse toward the edges. Field curvature means the best image lies on a curved surface that may not match the detector, and astigmatism makes off-axis stars look elliptical, a problem that grows fast across a wide field. Some designs fix part of this, either by reshaping the mirror surfaces, as the Ritchey–Chrétien telescope does, or by adding a correcting lens, as catadioptric telescopes do.
